evidence.note: Early on derives quantitative floor: 4096 element-rounds, valu bottleneck ceil(4096*3.0/6)=2048, ties SIMD width (VLEN=8) and slot limits (6 valu/cycle) to a minimum cycle estimate before writing the optimized kernel.

Builds explicit load-bottleneck model: 4096 tree loads / 2 load slots = 2048 cycle floor; hash bottleneck 512 groups × 9 cycles (with multiply_add fusion) / concurrency = 576-1152 cycles. Compares the two to identify the binding constraint.

Tracks slot occupancy explicitly as a cost metric — 1.68 ops/bundle (of 23 max) → 3.99 → 5.19 → 6.2 cycles/group vs theoretical ~4 — and uses the utilization gap to prioritize the next scheduler improvement.

Uses the gap between measured (2914) and floor to decide the next transform: recognizes that without grouping the floor is 2048 (so <1250 is impossible), computes grouping reduces loads 4096→870 giving ~1152-1250, and concludes grouping is the essential blocking transform.

Final submission reasoning restates the tight lower-bound model (load floor 2048, hash floor 1152, grouping-enabled ~1250) and correctly recognizes the kernel is near the no-grouping floor, explaining why it stalled at 2914.

reasoning: The agent consistently constructs an explicit quantitative cost model tying instruction counts, SIMD width, and slot limits to cycles (4096 loads / 2 slots = 2048 floor; hash 512 groups × 9 cycles / concurrency), tracks slot occupancy as a metric, and uses the measured-vs-floor gap to direct each optimization (pipelining, fusion, then grouping) — a clear directed descent rather than blind search, matching the level-8 anchor and reaching toward level-10. It also correctly recognizes when it is near the no-grouping floor and identifies grouping as the only remaining transform capable of closing the gap. It falls just short of a perfect 10 because the bound figures drift (1024 vs 1152 vs 1250) and it never fully integrates the hash critical path with the load bound into a single tight limit, so I place it at 9.
